THOUGHT: This 31-year-old woman presents with inflammatory joint symptoms (swelling, redness, warmth, tenderness, and stiffness) involving the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the fingers and the right knee — a pattern highly suggestive of asymmetric, oligoarticular arthritis. The DIP involvement is atypical for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), which typically affects proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints first and spares DIPs early on. Her negative rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies further make RA unlikely. Elevated ESR and CRP confirm systemic inflammation. Crucially, she has cutaneous and nail findings classic for psoriasis: nail pitting and cracking, and well-demarcated, rough, erythematous plaques over extensor surfaces (elbows). Skin biopsy confirms psoriasis. Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) commonly presents with dactylitis (though not explicitly described here, finger swelling + redness may reflect this), DIP predominance, enthesitis, and nail dystrophy — all present or strongly suggested. Family history of similar condition (father) supports genetic predisposition (e.g., HLA-B27 association, though not tested). Fatigue and functional impairment are consistent with active spondyloarthropathy. Other differential diagnoses — such as gout (unlikely without acute monoarticular onset, hyperuricemia, or tophi), reactive arthritis (no antecedent infection or urethritis/conjunctivitis), or lupus (no malar rash, photosensitivity, renal, or serologic markers like ANA/anti-dsDNA reported) — are less supported. The constellation of inflammatory musculoskeletal disease + psoriatic skin/nail changes + negative RF/anti-CCP + elevated acute-phase reactants strongly points to psoriatic arthritis.

DIAGNOSIS: Psoriatic arthritis
